First, let me say I have nothing against Minecraft, Mojang, or Notch (I play the game nearly every day). My reason for asking is pure curiosity. I'm a computer engineer by trade, so any necessary technicality is just fine.

I've been wondering about this for some time, for several reasons:

  • Studio: Minecraft was created mostly by a single developer, with little prior experience (and almost no budget); Terraria by a small team, etc.
  • Innovation: The core gameplay of Minecraft-like games is very simple (especially in 2D), excluding online multiplayer and other specific features
  • Inspiration: There are many (much) older games featuring environment/terrain modification (e.g. DigDug, Artillery) and RPG/crafting elements
  • Art: Models, textures, animations, movement, and combat are exceedingly simple by comparison to (even vintage) action platformers and fighting games
  • Tech: Minecraft is Java (poorly-optimized compared to raw-coded/compiled games), implying the modern "tech" requirements are mostly artificial
  • Size: Terrain and map sizes are far larger than necessary; the gameplay & appeal would be unchanged if smaller/simpler (using less RAM/HDD)

I'm specifically not considering 3D graphics (voxels/cubes vs. arxels/squares) as a requirement, due to the success of 2D mine/craft games (Terraria, Starbound, etc) which easily preserve the core appeal and gameplay of their 3D counterparts. I'm also already aware of Infiniminer, which predates Minecraft but lacks its RPG elements.
ELI5: Why did it take until 2009/2011 to create a game like Minecraft (or Terraria)? Couldn't this simple pixel/block gameplay have been implemented on some of the earliest consoles, decades ago?

I don't think pixel art had the same status back then. The focus was on increasing realism not retro charm.

This is an excellent point. I would also venture that gaming mechanics weren't sophisticated enough to have a game that was focussed solely on crafting. Either that, or nobody had the idea to focus on it exclusively in a game until Minecraft.

Because nobody that could make it thought of it. It's really that simple. It's not that it was too difficult to make, or that there were any kind of limitations.

Nobody that was in a position to create it thought of it. Or, if they did, it wasn't in the right place at the right time like Minecraft was. There were probably 'clones' before Minecraft that just didn't take off. Though Minecraft would be the clone, in this case.

There are a lot of factors that contribute to it, but if I wanted to pick the most important one I'd say that game development has gotten a lot more accessible to creative hobbyists and solo devs. Minecraft is actually very taxing on hardware since it stores massive arrays of voxel data, and the game logic for rendering and updating is very complex given it was written by 1 person.

If it were not for fast computers, the availability of high level languages like Java, and simple easy to use managed graphics libraries like LWJGL it would have probably required an entire team of people and lots of funding to produce. Simply put, without all of these recent advancements in programming languages, hardware, and graphics APIs it would have been a LOT harder to make a game like minecraft, which means it would have had to go past publishers and investors and board members etc.

Since minecraft we have seen the rise of even more advanced high level tools like Unity and Cryengine and UDK which allows almost anyone to realize their unique ideas with much less skills and smaller team sizes.

A Brief Note Regarding Format

I would like responses to discuss the points raised by their consequences. If you disagree with the explanations I provide, please help me improve upon them by providing examples, real or reasoned, in which the proposed solutions are erroneous or inadequate.

First Dilemma: Who Are We?

  • Digg became a graveyard of advertisements. Reddit, low effort repeat content, quote chains, radfem harassment (hello again SRS), meta-brigading (Hello Best/Worst of), etc. Who we want to become depends on the following dilemmas, their validity, and solutions.

Second Dilemma: Votes & Effects

  • We trend toward the behavior of voting based on agreement, not discussion value.

  • Trolls feed off negativity. The more downvotes they gather, the more they are encouraged to continue posting.

  • It encourages quick approval or assent, sometimes in massive quantities, with no ability to raise objections.

  • "Brigading", even from within a sub, is used to silence dissent without discussion by eliminating visibility. Such as rapidly downvoating unread same-user posts in a thread chain.

Possible Solutions

  • Hide votes, not only in comments, but on personal pages. The latter prevents trolls from being fed, the former prevents brigades from picking up steam. Additionally, it encourages further participation of unpopular dissent by hiding mass knee-jerk disapproval.

  • Limit votes. I believe it was the worst decision to increase votes allotted, and far better to encourage quality content by restricting votes perpetually to discourage low-effort participation.

  • Disallow voting except from within a comment thread ("Permalink") to encourage people to read whole discussion threads. OR by only within the subreddit.

Consequences

  • By limiting votes, low-effort participation declines, in turn limiting potential advertisement revenue. However, it makes brigading less tenable.

  • By hiding votes, it becomes impossible to determine ones communal standing except by active participants.

  • By voting only within a full comment thread, Participation within threads increases while voting in general declines.

Third Dilemma: Advertisement/Shills

  • Advertisers come in many forms, including political. These can use various vote gaming services (which pay people to vote on content), buzzword clickbait, etc.

  • Shills that are not known to be can mislead communities by clever rhetoric, gaming the social side of things instead of paying for ad space.

Possible Solutions

  • Encourage Advertisers and Shills to publicly mark themselves as such, like with a [Shill] tag, so they can participate actively in the community relevant to their given service or product. Do this by making it an option that can be purchased, like ad space the community can vote on. This benefits all parties by gaining more revenue and, ideally, longer term advertising partners the community enjoys personally. All while adding a public face that can be scrutinized as needed.

Consequences

  • Ad revenue of this nature is volatile, but benefits smaller services or products by potentially cheaper ad "submissions" to compensate for the fact the community may entirely reject. These submissions must also obey the same visibility rules as regular members.

Fourth Dilemma: New Content

  • "New" pages tend to lack "Knights". This means the majority of content is delivered by a minority of dedicated voters, effectively controlling the visibility of content.

  • Most people ignore the "New" page entirely.

Possible Solution

  • Require voting in "New" to earn votes for elsewhere, and allow subs to set time limits on how long you must subscribe to access the New page.

Consequences

  • It is more likely the majority of a given sub will decide on what content they see, as well as see more of what might've been unseen.

  • With the publicly tagged ad or shill, this allows more people to decide whether they like the product or service.

  • It decreases the number of low-effort participants even further, resulting in more lurking.

Fifth Dilemma: Subvoats & Usernames

  • As we see on Reddit, a mod can end up moderator of dozens (or even hundreds) of communities.

  • We grab communities with no intention of actually modding them legitimately (A Voat user has /SRS grabbed for this purpose).

  • People grab names (GabeN, anyone?) for their popular use and, invariably, squat them with no activity.

Possible Solution

  • Make an appeal process for claiming names and subs on the basis of their inactivity (X years inactive).

Cryptocurrencies are pretty common nowadays; and making them isn't that difficult a task. I worked on the Dogecoin Core, and can assure you that the magical logistics that are held within the btc codebase aren't actually as magical (but they are quite logical), as one may think.

We have a quickly growing community on here - and could easily build a nice CPU/GPU-Friendly crypto solution for us to mine and trade with. Targeting a CPU/GPU friendly algorithm will ensure that we have a level playing field (basically, anyone can mine without giant electricity bills, without having to buy ASICs as is the case with BTC/LTC/Doge); and we can set the coin so that a 1% premine is donated directly to Voat.

Most cryptos unfortunately don't hit BTC/LTC/Doge levels (where 1% would actually be over $1mil USD) - but it's very likely that we could net Voat a few thousand bucks (or even upwards of $10k), simply by mining, promoting, and trading the coin ourselves. Outside of a 1% premine for Voat, it would be nice to set aside another 1% to give away in competitions, or as bounties for developers making new apps and the likes; but it's definitely not necessary. I believe we have a tight enough community right now that devs would be happy to contribute, in order to simply grow the service.

Voat themselves could choose to segment the 1% premine; i.e: reward users for submitting good content with a small amount of coins, rather than the current revenue share model they're running with. This will allow Voat to continue rewarding contributors, without having to take away real cash from their reserves, which are obviously much needed for expanding their server capacity at the moment.

If enough people are interested in such a thing, I'd be happy to set up a subverse, and get coding on the coin. We'd need to ensure a set launch date, alongside making sure that we've plenty of self-help guides available for those who are uninitiated to crypto mining.

This is something I always wanted to see in Reddit. It would have been the best added feature IMO, had it happened. I think we need to take some ideas out of our real lives to apply this. I have a pretty good idea about how to get this done which will not depend on who is subscribed to which subverse or Admin intervention. It will be a system by the Voaters, for the Voaters.

Similar to how nations have a system of law in hierarchy, we can have a hierarchy of moderation. It will have similarities to governmental systems but will not copy any one government exactly. It will require help from the admins to implement. I think a rough outline can be as follows:

Atko is the King. This is his land and he rules it as he sees fit. We will trust him to be a good king and rule it wisely.

Admins are similar to national supreme court justices here in the US. They don't get voted in or out. They are appointed and are in for life or until they resign. They have full control over how the site operates and have final say on all matters. The rest goes without saying as they are more or less employees of the website. We will also trust them.

We will develop a new subverse which will be similar to a jurisdictional court, however the jurisdiction will be the entire website. This subverse will be in charge of checking the moderation team of other subverses. Similar to a supreme court, they have override abilities to the moderation team of a subverse, but only by an appeals system. They must not interfere with the goings on of a subverse unless addressed by users of Voat. Even in these cases, they will be called upon to decide appropriate courses of action based on 1) The general rules of Voat, 2) The general rules of the subverse, 3) What seems fair to them based on the rights of the users (after all, all rules need to be addressed occasionally to determine their continued effectiveness).

These will basically be the moderators of the moderation teams of subverses. Their responsibility will be to the userbase, not subordinate moderation teams. They will be voted on by the userbase as a whole on an interval which is yet to be determined. They will carry an UNLIMITED amount of term possibilities (This is important). The reason for this is because here on the internet, things move faster than real life. Changes are passed in a matter of days/weeks rather than years/decades. We only need the best moderators for this job, regardless of how long they've been doing the job. If we impose term caps on this position, changes can/may be made so quickly that it may distort the overall view and direction of Voat. We need moderators here who are effective at keeping and sustaining the core values of the site. To do this we may need a moderator who has been here for years. This moderation team will be checked/balanced by the userbase as a whole by voting. They will convene at an interval yet to be determined or at any time necessary between that interval. This moderation team will have a specified amount of moderators. Decisions will be passed based on a minimum amount of votes, and a majority system. Any moderators inactive for an undetermined period of time may be relieved of their position.

The moderators of this subverse will NOT be called for the following reasons:

  • Unbanning a user from a subverse (however a user may be unbanned as a result of related action)
  • Taking posts out of any spam filter
  • Implementing new rules/regulations to a subverse
  • Deciding an overall plan for a subverse and what type for content the subverse will contain
  • etc.

They WILL be called for the following:

  • Deciding whether current policies in a subverse are generally unfair to the userbase as a whole and repealing them if necessary
  • Deciding whether a specific moderator or moderation team is infringing on basic rights of the userbase
  • Deciding whether a specific moderator or moderation team is abusing their power and must be relieved of their position
  • etc.

Another idea would be to have this moderation team be responsible for multiple moderation teams under this one, but above the subverse moderators, who are responsible for a number of subverses based on the # of subscribers. These moderation teams would also have unlimited term caps and be voted on at an interval which is yet to be determined, and not necessarily the same as the moderation team above it. This reason is twofold:

  • Subverses with a larger amount of subscribers may operate differently than subverses with a smaller amount of subscribers
  • To alleviate the load of a huge amount of subverses all on one moderation team and to spread out the work

This idea can be implemented immediately or at a time in which the load of the website has grown and this system is needed.

The last group of moderators would be subverse specific. This group would function the same way it operates now. They will be chosen and kept as the subverse sees fit but will ultimately be responsible for the userbase as a whole and will answer to the moderation team directly superior to them.

This system will serve as a method to have subverses act independently but still be responsible for their actions. It will allow for a system of balance between the users and moderators.

Subverses will NOT fall into the jurisdiction of any moderation team below the admins if:

  • They have UNDER a specified amount of subscribers (amount yet to be determined)
  • They are operated by a single user for his/her own purposes (Ex: compiled works of that user). The subverse in question would have to be moderated BY the user in which it is about, however.
  • It is private (other limitations may apply)

This system can be modified before and after it is put in place. The intent and purpose of this system is NOT so that things will stay the same indefinitely. All things must change with the times. The intent and purpose for this system IS for consistency in fairness to the users.

An option would also be to have a subverse which will act as a council to make changes to and oversee this system. The council will be in charge of adding/removing checking/balancing the moderation team directly below the admins, but will NOT have any jurisdiction over any decisions made regarding the oversight of subverses directly nor make any changes to any subverses. The council will SOLELY be in charge of modifying and upholding the system. The council will be in charge of making decisions based on any discrepancy of the system. The council will be voted in and will have an undetermined amount of term limits (an unlimited term cap is a possibility, however an alternative term cap may be imposed). The council may convene at an interval yet to be determined or at any time necessary between that interval. This council will have a specified amount of moderators. Decisions will be passed based on a minimum amount of votes, and a majority system. Any moderators inactive for an undetermined period of time may be relieved of their position.

Please discuss. Any thoughts regarding this system are appreciated. Maybe we can work something like this into place. I know it sounds complicated and time consuming, but the idea is that 1) It will work as a system which checks itself and is best for the users, and 2) hopefully will not be as time consuming as one would hope as responsibilities are displaced on their respective moderation team.
